turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Pop him on the chair, love. I got a temperature of thirty eight point two, pulse one hundred and twenty, sats ninety eight, and respirations twenty four. He wouldn't keep still for a blood pressure.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Hello Alfie, I'm Dr Shah. Dad, tell me what's been happening.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been burning up, and this cough, proper chesty. We were up half the night with it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three days. Cough started Sunday evening, then the temperature kicked in Monday.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): When I phoned Mum she said the cough's been a full week, from last Monday.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She wasn't there. It's three days, not a week. She always adds a bit on.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so three days from you, about a week from Mum. I'll note it as roughly three days to a week. Alfie, how're you feeling?
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): I want the green dinosaur sticker. Not the baby one. My teacher has a lizard called Pickle.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll do stickers in a minute. Does your tummy hurt at all?
[SEG0011] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. How high has the fever been at home?
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Forehead thermometer said thirty nine point four last night. His mum texted forty, but that gadget always reads high, I don't buy it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what have you actually given him?
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Calpol, the strawberry one. One five mil spoon this morning, same again last night. Well, actually, last night might've been a bit before bed, same spoon though.
[SEG0016] person_1 (NURSE): Mum told me two spoons, ten mils of Calpol, and that she'd given the orange Nurofen at lunch as well.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, I measured it, five mils, not ten. I didn't give any Nurofen. She might've done yesterday while I was at work, I genuinely don't know.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the Calpol amount is muddy, five versus ten, and whether he had Nurofen is up in the air. Any wheeze, or is he working hard to breathe?
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No wheeze. The cough's dry, actually, not chesty like I said, comes in bursts and it's worse at night. He's drinking. Not eating much.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any rash, vomiting, diarrhoea?
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No rash, no diarrhoea. He gags when he coughs but he hasn't been sick.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alfie, does your head hurt? What about your ears?
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Ears are fine. Pickle eats crickets. Can he come to the doctors?
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Maybe another day. Dad, runny nose, sore throat?
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bit of a runny nose, clear. He said his throat was scratchy yesterday, hasn't mentioned it today.
[SEG0026] person_4 (PATIENT): My tummy hurts. It's squirmy, like when Pickle wiggles. I didn't want my toast.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you said. When did that squirmy feeling start?
[SEG0028] person_4 (PATIENT): Um. After the toast. Or before. I don't know.

[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's six, well, six in March, so five, hang on, he turned six in March, he's six. Not usually poorly, no asthma, no eczema, jabs up to date. We don't smoke, and he lives with me and his mum.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): None that we know of.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to his chest and have a look at his throat. Alfie, big breaths, like you're blowing out birthday candles.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no crackles and no wheeze. Throat's a little red. Tummy's soft, mildly tender in the middle, no guarding. Ears look fine.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely a viral infection, fever and a cough, nothing focal in the chest. Tummy ache often tags along in children. I can't fully rule out an early throat infection.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So, um, does he need antibiotics then?

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. Carry on with paracetamol, the Calpol Six Plus, five mils by mouth up to four times a day, that's the right dose now he's six. You can add ibuprofen, the orange Nurofen, seven point five mils by mouth three times a day if the fever's making him miserable, with a bit of food. Don't guess with spoons.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep fluids going, little and often. If he's struggling to breathe, if the fever's still raging, or if a rash comes up that doesn't fade when you press it, come back straight away or go to A&E. Otherwise I'll see you in three days.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three days, yeah. Do I book that outside?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please, reception will put it in. You did really well, Alfie.
[SEG0040] person_4 (PATIENT): Green dinosaur. And Pickle says bye. Bye lizard.
[SEG0041] person_1 (NURSE): Green one's yours. We'll grab that appointment on the way out.

spec.situation: Parent brings a toddler or school-age child with fever and cough; the two parents (or parent and grandparent) disagree about how long, how high, and what was given (paracetamol vs ibuprofen, doses by 'spoon'). Child says only a few words.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

Runny nose was described as clear.

Chest examination was clear / nothing focal in the chest, not just absence of crackles and wheeze.
Safety-netting included not to guess doses with spoons.
Ibuprofen was advised to be given with a bit of food.
